subject: Civil Engineering
title: Flood Frequency Analysis
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Flood Frequency Analysis.

hook.text: A '100-year flood' doesn't happen once a century — it has a 1% chance every single year.

buildup.text: Engineers collect decades of stream flow data and rank the floods by magnitude.

discovery.text: Statistical distributions — like Log-Pearson Type III — fit curves to the data.

twist.text: Climate change is shifting the statistics. Yesterday's 100-year flood becomes a 50-year event.

climax.text: Bridge openings, dam spillways, and levees are all sized to a design flood frequency.

punchline.text: Floods are random, but engineers size defenses by probability, not luck.

quiz.question: What does a '100-year flood' actually mean?
options: It will occur exactly once every 100 years
There is a 1% probability of it occurring in any given year
It is the largest flood ever recorded at that location

details.summary: Flood frequency analysis uses statistical methods to estimate the magnitude of floods for various return periods based on historical flow records. Engineers fit probability distributions to annual maximum flow data to predict flood levels that infrastructure must withstand over its design life.
details.whyItMatters: Flood frequency estimates directly determine the height of levees, capacity of bridges, and crest elevation of dams. Underestimation causes catastrophic failure; overestimation wastes enormous construction resources.
takeaways: Log-Pearson Type III is the standard distribution used by US agencies for flood frequency
Longer historical records produce more reliable flood frequency estimates
Climate change is making historical flood records less reliable for future predictions

faq.question: How reliable are flood frequency estimates for very rare events?
faq.answer: Reliability decreases dramatically for events exceeding the length of the historical record. Estimating a 500-year flood from 50 years of data involves large statistical uncertainty. Regional methods combining data from multiple nearby stations improve estimates.

faq.question: Why might historical flood records no longer represent future flood risk?
faq.answer: Climate change alters precipitation patterns, producing more intense storms. Urbanization increases impervious area and peak runoff. Land use changes modify watershed response. Dam construction and removal change downstream flows.
